solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: It’s ‘ruined by the abrader’ ?

indicators.note: Letters that are ruined have been wrecked out of their proper order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A garment worn to nothing by something that scrapes it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and the quoted words also rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth rubbed away by an abrader ends up worn thin, which is what threadbare means.

clue.text: Sort of expert breaking the ice

indicators.note: Breaking the words smashes their letters into a new order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A specialist who knows how to get conversation going at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: "Breaking the ice" reads as a single idiom, but "breaking" is the instruction and "the ice" is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a techie is a particular sort of expert, one who specialises in computers and gadgets.

clue.text: Edit revolutionary piece of legislation

blocks.note: A red is a revolutionary, a communist.
An Act of Parliament is a piece of legislation.

explanation.surface: Amending a radical new law.
explanation.walkthrough: "Revolutionary" suggests turning something round, but here it simply gives RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: redacting is editing a document, usually to cut sensitive material before it is released.

clue.text: Taking a direct line with sales force needing to be sorted out

indicators.note: Something needing sorting out is currently in a muddle and must be rearranged.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A manager takes a firm line with an unruly sales team.
explanation.walkthrough: "With" looks like a link word, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: As the crow flies means by the straightest route, taking a direct line.

clue.text: Be without post after First in Biochemistry? It’s a crime!

indicators.note: The first in Biochemistry is its opening letter.

blocks.note: The first letter of Biochemistry.
To lack something is to be without it.
Post and mail are the same thing.

explanation.surface: A student who got a First in Biochemistry but still cannot find a job.
explanation.walkthrough: "First" reads as the degree class, a First in Biochemistry, but it tells you to take the opening letter; "after" puts the rest behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: blackmail, extorting money by threats, is one example of a crime.

clue.text: In summary, harvest has been interrupted by cold

definitions.note: RECAP is a summary; 'in summary' is the phrase that introduces one.

indicators.note: Something interrupted has another thing thrust into its middle.

blocks.note: To reap is to harvest.
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap.

explanation.surface: A farming report: the harvest was held up by cold weather.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes into the middle of REAP.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun RECAP means a summary, so 'in summary' points to it loosely as the phrase used to introduce one.

clue.text: Capital city that is held by king very briefly

indicators.note: What is held by something sits inside its grasp.

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king.
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is.
v. is the short form of very.

explanation.surface: A capital that a monarch controlled for only a short time.
explanation.walkthrough: IE sits between K and V, the two parts of "king very briefly".
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Kiev, now usually spelt Kyiv, is the capital of Ukraine, one instance of a capital city.

clue.text: Unfortunate home — middle of floor is in a state

indicators.note: The middle of floor is its central letter.

blocks.note: Ill as in ill luck, unfortunate.
To be in is to be at home.
The middle letter of FLOOR, taken as one of its two central Os.
Taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A sad home whose floor has fallen into a terrible state of repair.
explanation.walkthrough: "In a state" sounds like disrepair; "in" is only the link and "a state" is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Illinois is one of the fifty United States, so it is one instance of a state.

clue.text: There’s little good in dreadful avarice evident in minister’s home

indicators.note: Dreadful avarice is avarice in a terrible state, its letters mangled.
Little good goes in the jumbled word.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.
G is the short form of good.

explanation.surface: A scandal: greed found in the house of a clergyman, with hardly any good there.
explanation.walkthrough: "Little good" sounds like a moral judgment on the minister, but it just means the abbreviation G.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicarage is the house of a vicar, a Church of England minister.

clue.text: Irishmen did not get confused by modern TV feature exciting viewers?

indicators.note: Things that get confused are jumbled up.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: Some Irish viewers were baffled by a new gimmick on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: 3D television was the new way to thrill viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: The third dimension, depth, is what 3D TV adds to the picture.

clue.text: Trainee given whip, having collected low exam grades

indicators.note: Something that has collected other things holds them inside.

blocks.note: The cat-o'-nine-tails is a whip.
D and E are low grades in an exam.

explanation.surface: A recruit who did poorly in his exams is punished with a whipping.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat-o'-nine-tails, a knotted whip once used for flogging, is the usual crossword meaning of cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a trainee in the armed forces or police.

clue.text: Cocoa I’ll have initially drunk — I really want the harder stuff!

definitions.text: Cocoa I’ll have initially drunk — I really want the harder stuff!
definitions.note: The whole clue is what the answer would say, not a noun phrase.

indicators.note: Initially means take the first letter of have.
Letters that are drunk stagger about out of order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.
The first letter of have.

explanation.surface: Someone offered a cup of cocoa sips it but longs for something stronger.
explanation.walkthrough: "Drunk" seems to mean the cocoa was swallowed, but it is telling you to scramble the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: &lit: the whole clue is the voice of someone who drinks cocoa only for want of anything better, craving strong drink as an alcoholic does.

clue.text: Like someone wearing tartan unable to act?

blocks.note: Tartan is a pattern of criss-crossing stripes, so its wearer is clad in that squared pattern.
Restrained or held back, as a chess king under attack must deal with the threat before anything else.

explanation.walkthrough: Tartan is a checked cloth, so its wearer is dressed in check. Held in check means restrained.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone held in check is kept back and unable to act freely.

clue.text: One who is sleeping won’t be doing much for the business

definitions.text: One who is sleeping won’t be doing much for the business

blocks.note: reads as someone literally asleep, and so idle

blocks.clueFragment: won’t be doing much for the business
blocks.note: the setter means an investor who puts money into a firm but takes no active role in it

explanation.walkthrough: A sleeping partner puts money into a business but takes no active part in running it.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue describes a sleeping partner, so the answer is PARTNER.

clue.text: Promising to study quietly inside when there’s heavy stuff to digest

indicators.note: The study words go inside the word for promising.

blocks.note: A budding talent is a promising one.
To read a subject is to study it.
P, piano, is the musical direction for quiet.

explanation.surface: A student promises to revise quietly at home when faced with a dense textbook.
explanation.walkthrough: "Heavy stuff to digest" sounds like difficult reading, but it is a stodgy food.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic paraphrase: the dessert is stodgy and hard on the stomach, while 'digest' also plays on taking in heavy reading.

clue.text: Gape naughtily, having got there after flipping?

definitions.text: Gape naughtily, having got there after flipping?

indicators.note: Letters behaving naughtily will not stay in their places.
Flipping the letters tosses them into a new order.

blocks.note: The first fodder, taken as printed.
The second fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A reader leafs through a tabloid and stares at what they find.
explanation.walkthrough: Page Three of the Sun, a British tabloid, carried a photo of a topless model; readers flipped pages to reach it and gaped.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes someone flipping to Page Three and ogling it.

clue.text: Pay tribute to soldiers, joined by MP maybe

blocks.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, are soldiers.
An MP is a Member of Parliament, one kind of member.

explanation.surface: A politician joins troops at a ceremony honouring the fallen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes Remembrance Day, when soldiers and politicians honour the war dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the commemorative sense: to remember the war dead is to honour them publicly.

clue.text: Older egg is bad? Nonsense!

indicators.note: A bad egg is spoilt, and spoilt letters lose their order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the claim that an old egg has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: "Nonsense!" reads as an exclamation of disbelief but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggerel is badly written verse, and by extension nonsense.

clue.text: Pursuit of public schoolboys with abnormally low mental age

indicators.note: Abnormally arranged letters are not in their usual order.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A dig at posh schoolboys and their childish games.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is an elite British public school, meaning a private fee-paying one; the Wall Game is a muddy football game played only there.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the game is a sport, or pursuit, played only by the boys of that one public school.

clue.text: Public revenue’s beginning to fail — is serenity curtailed?

definitions.note: FISCAL is an adjective; the possessive stands in as 'of public revenue'.

indicators.note: The beginning of fail is its first letter.
Curtailed means docked of its tail, the last letter.

blocks.note: The first letter of fail.
Taken as printed.
CALM, serenity, without its last letter.

explanation.surface: A worried question about whether falling tax income will end the calm.
explanation.walkthrough: CALM loses its final M.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiscal means relating to public revenue, such as taxes.

clue.text: Day the heavens may appear to be lively

blocks.note: FRI is the short form of Friday, a day.
The sky is the heavens.

explanation.surface: On a bright day the sky itself seems full of life.
explanation.walkthrough: Any day could be meant; the answer needs the three-letter abbreviation for Friday.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a frisky animal or person is playful and full of energy.

clue.text: Get flung around in middle of mess produced by floods

indicators.note: Flung around means the letters are thrown about into a new order.
The middle of mess is its two central letters.
The shuffled word goes in between the middle letters.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.
The two middle letters of MESS.

explanation.surface: Someone is thrown about in the chaos of a flood.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled FLUNG sits between E and S. "Get" just starts the instruction and gives no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To engulf is to swamp or flood, so engulfs means floods.

clue.text: Brown bit of flower cut short, one inside

indicators.note: Cut short means lose the final letter.
The one goes inside the shortened word.

blocks.note: A sepal is part of a flower; cut short it is SEPA.
I is the Roman numeral for one.

explanation.surface: A gardener describes a wilted brown petal snipped from a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: SEPAL loses its L, then I goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sepia is a warm brown shade, named after the cuttlefish ink it was first made from.

clue.text: Port sending granite abroad

indicators.note: Abroad in the old sense of widely scattered, with the letters strewn about.

blocks.note: The fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: A harbour ships stone overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: "Port" might be the wine or the left side of a ship; here it is a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Tangier is a harbour city in Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, one instance of a port.

clue.text: One holds booze in chest protected by electronic sounding device

indicators.note: Something protected by another thing is wrapped up inside it.

blocks.note: A beeper is an electronic device that makes a sound.
An ark is a chest, as in the Ark of the Covenant.

explanation.surface: Someone hides drink in a locked chest wired with an alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: "Chest" suggests a torso or a box for drink, but it is the old word for a sacred box, as in the Ark of the Covenant.
explanation.definitionFit: A barkeeper runs a bar and holds its stock of drink.

clue.text: Indian people invading mountain castle

indicators.note: The answer has invaded the next words, sitting inside them.

blocks.note: Inside mountaIN CAStle.

explanation.surface: Natives storm a fortress in the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: "Indian" means American Indian here, not from India.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were the native people of the Andes in South America.

clue.text: Part of actor‘s register in speech

definitions.note: The definition is an actor's part.

indicators.note: In speech means the word is spoken rather than spelt.

blocks.note: A roll is a register of names.

explanation.surface: A comment on an actor's vocal range.
explanation.walkthrough: "Register" suggests voice pitch, but here it is a list of names, a roll.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the character an actor plays is called their part.

clue.text: Navy led by head that’s friend acting like a father

blocks.note: The pate is the top of the head.
RN is the Royal Navy.
An ally is a friend.

explanation.surface: A naval commander who is a friend and father figure to the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: "Head" means the crown of the head here, an old word crosswords use often; "led by" puts it in front of the Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to behave paternally is to act in a fatherly, protective way.
